# Findings

## What was measured

The pilot asked whether a different grate cover might shorten the time water stayed above the pavement after rain. We observed six drains on two streets during eight storms: four before a cover change and four after. The three drains on the lower street received the new covers. The three on the upper street kept their original covers. Cover allocation was not random. The lower street was chosen because crews had received more complaints there.

For each drain in each storm, a fixed camera recorded the minutes that water stood above a painted reference line. A duration of zero means no visible water above that line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations (6 drains × 8 storms) were available.

| Street | Cover change | Mean minutes above line, before (12 observations) | Mean minutes above line, after (12 observations) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lower | New covers | 18 | 10 | −8 |
| Upper | Original covers | 9 | 7 | −2 |

Recorded durations were shorter at both sets of drains in the later period, and the reduction was larger on the lower street. This is a description of the recordings. It may help in deciding what to study next, but it does not by itself identify an effect of the cover.

## What the measurements cannot explain

Several factors changed or varied alongside the covers, and the pilot cannot separate them:

- **Non-random allocation.** The lower street was selected because it had more complaints, and it also started with longer durations (18 minutes against 9). The two streets may differ in ways that affect both ponding and how they change over time, so the comparison between them is not a like-for-like test.
- **Rainfall.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier four. Neither street had its own gauge, and the pilot has no within-storm intensity measurements. Lighter rain alone could produce shorter durations at both sets of drains, and we cannot say how much of the change it accounts for.
- **Simultaneous cleaning.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. The initial quantity of leaves was not recorded. We therefore cannot say that cleaning explains why the lower street improved more, and we cannot rule it out. Cleaning both streets does not make it irrelevant, because the lower street may have had more debris to remove.

## What was not measured

The camera records show shorter durations above the line. They should not be read as evidence of the following:

- **Drainage capacity.** It was not directly measured, so an increase in capacity is not established.
- **Flooded properties.** The pilot made no property-damage observations, and fewer flooded properties is not something these data can show.
- **Peak water depth.** A change in peak depth could matter even if duration did not change, but depth was not extracted from the images.

## Reliability of the duration measure

Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. We have not tested whether different scorers assign the same duration to the same recording, so the consistency of the measure is unknown.

## Possible follow-up design

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and the amount of debris before cleaning. That would address some of the ambiguities above, though rotation alone would not make storms identical. Separately, a scorer-agreement check would show whether the camera-based duration measure is dependable.

## What the existing recordings can support

The recordings remain useful for describing these eight storms and for assessing whether camera-based duration is a practical measure. They do not establish that the new covers shortened ponding.

This evaluation compared two ways of placing diagrams on a worksheet about why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and a wide vessel. Version A placed a diagram beside each question. Version B grouped the same diagrams on a reference page. The wording, diagrams, and question order were otherwise identical.

Four classes used the worksheets during one lesson: two used A and two used B. Teachers chose their classes’ versions before seeing pupil responses. There were 52 returned worksheets for A and 49 for B. Six additional pupils assigned A and five assigned B were absent. Only returned worksheets were analysed.

Teachers used the same written instructions but could answer pupils’ questions during the lesson. Those exchanges were not recorded. Pupil assignment and teacher assistance therefore could not be treated as controlled features of the comparison.

A scorer who could not see the worksheet layout assessed transcribed answers to the final explanation question. Answers received one point for stating that the amount of water was unchanged and one for explaining that vessel shape changed the water level.

|---|---:|---:|
| Two points | 31 | 27 |
| One point | 15 | 16 |
| Zero points | 6 | 6 |
| Total returned worksheets | 52 | 49 |

These scores describe responses to one question; they do not measure pupils’ general understanding of volume. No earlier baseline task was scored, so the groups’ starting knowledge is unknown.

A second scorer independently scored ten transcribed answers. The scorers agreed on nine, and discussion resolved the tenth before the final totals were compiled. This small check supports the description of the scoring procedure but does not constitute a complete reliability study.

It also provides no evidence about pupils’ layout preferences, because no preference question was asked. The completed evaluation offers a concrete comparison of the returned answers and identifies information that a more controlled evaluation would need to record.

# Briefing: Automatic Flood Warning Signs for the Underpass

## Recommendation

Install the proposed automatic warning signs, on condition that the same decision also:

1. names a team responsible for monthly sensor checks, and
2. provides a manual closure procedure for when the system is unavailable.

Staff time for these checks has not yet been allocated. Until it is, the purchase is not ready for approval. Leaving the condition implicit would be misleading.

## What the signs do and do not do

The underpass sometimes fills with water before a maintenance crew can close the road. The signs address that delay by warning drivers sooner. They will not keep water out. Installing them would complete a warning project, not the flood work, and the drainage problem would remain unresolved.

Because signs cannot prevent every unsafe entry, some drivers will still overlook or disregard them. That is not a reason to reject warning equipment. It is a reason to describe accurately what the equipment does.

## Cost and comparison with pipe replacement

- Installing two signs is estimated at 18,000 units of local currency.
- Replacing the drainage pipe is estimated at 140,000.
- Neither estimate includes annual maintenance.

The signs are a smaller initial purchase, but they are not a measured substitute for the pipe. We have no agreed estimate of how much either option would reduce injuries or vehicle damage. The signs should be judged as a response to delayed warnings, not as a cheaper way to achieve the same outcome as the pipe.

## Why the maintenance and closure conditions matter

The signs activate when a water-level sensor crosses a set threshold. The sensor can fail, and the signs need power. A dark sign therefore cannot safely be read as "the road is clear," since it may mean the system is unavailable.

The proposal includes a permanent notice telling drivers that water may be present even when the electronic sign is off. This helps, but it does not solve the problem of drivers missing or ignoring warnings. Monthly sensor checks reduce the chance that the system is silently down. The manual closure procedure covers the periods when it is.

Pipe replacement remains a separate option that requires design work. Buying signs should not be described as approving or rejecting it.

There is a reasonable concern that a visible new device will reduce pressure to fix the drainage itself. We can answer part of that concern by requiring the next infrastructure report to state the pipe project's status explicitly. A reporting requirement cannot guarantee construction, and this briefing does not claim that it can.

 = Σ_j (μ_j − c) · Σ_{ω∈G_j} P({ω}) (X(ω) − μ_j)
 = Σ_j (μ_j − c) · 0 = 0,

where the factor (μ_j − c) comes out of the inner sum because it does not depend on ω ∈ G_j, and the inner sum is zero by (1). Every cell is covered, including those with p_j = 0.

**Step 3: the identity.** Pointwise,

X − c = (X − M) + (M − c),

(X − c)² = (X − M)² + 2(X − M)(M − c) + (M − c)².

Taking expectations (a finite sum, so linearity applies) and using Step 2,

E[(X − c)²] = E[(X − M)²] + 2·0 + E[(M − c)²] = E[(X − M)²] + E[(M − c)²].

**Step 4: the inequality and the equality condition.** Since E[(M − c)²] ≥ 0, we get E[(X − c)²] ≥ E[(X − M)²]. Because all quantities are finite, Step 3 gives

E[(X − c)²] − E[(X − M)²] = E[(M − c)²] = Σ_j p_j (μ_j − c)².

Equality holds exactly when this sum is zero. Every term is nonnegative, so the sum is zero exactly when p_j (μ_j − c)² = 0 for every j. This means μ_j = c for every cell with p_j > 0.

Now {M ≠ c} is the union of the cells with μ_j ≠ c, so

P(M ≠ c) = Σ_{j: μ_j ≠ c} p_j.

This is zero exactly when every cell with μ_j ≠ c has p_j = 0, which is the condition just derived. Hence equality holds if and only if M = c with probability one.

This is the second place the zero-probability cells matter. A cell with p_j = 0 may have μ_j = 0 ≠ c because of the convention, yet it neither breaks equality nor contributes to either side. So the equality condition must be stated as "M = c almost surely," not "M = c on every cell." ∎

**Summary of the repair.** The independence claim is replaced by the cell-wise identity (1) together with the fact that M is constant on cells. Together these give E[(X−M)(M−c)] = 0 directly. The zero-probability cells are used twice: to prove (1) when p_j = 0, and to read the equality condition as holding with probability one.

**Proof.** Write $P(\omega)=P(\{\omega\})$. Every expectation is a finite sum over $\Omega$, and since $G_1,\dots,G_m$ partition $\Omega$, each sum can be split over the cells. In particular, for any function $Y$,
$$
\mathbb E[Y]=\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\omega)\,Y(\omega).
$$

**Step 1: the residual has zero weighted sum on each cell.** We show that for every $j$,
$$
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\omega)\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)=0. \tag{1}
$$
Suppose first that $p_j>0$. By the definition of $\mu_j$,
$$
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\omega)X(\omega)=p_j\mu_j,
\qquad
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\omega)\mu_j=p_j\mu_j,
$$
so the difference is zero. Now suppose $p_j=0$. Then $\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\omega)=0$ and every term is nonnegative, so $P(\omega)=0$ for each $\omega\in G_j$. Every term in (1) is then zero.

**Step 2: the cross term vanishes.** On $G_j$ the function $M$ equals the constant $\mu_j$, so $M-c=\mu_j-c$ can be pulled out of the sum over $G_j$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\bigl[(X-M)(M-c)\bigr]
&=\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\omega)\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)(\mu_j-c)\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\omega)\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=0,
\end{aligned}
$$
where the last line uses (1). This uses only the definition of $\mu_j$ and the fact that $M$ is constant on each cell. No independence of $X-M$ and $M$ is needed or claimed. For a cell with $p_j=0$, the value $\mu_j=0$ is arbitrary, but it does not matter, because every $P(\omega)$ in that cell is zero.

**Step 3: the identity.** Pointwise,
$$
X-c=(X-M)+(M-c),
$$
so
$$
(X-c)^2=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2.
$$
Taking expectations and using Step 2 to drop the middle term gives
$$
\mathbb E\bigl[(X-c)^2\bigr]=\mathbb E\bigl[(X-M)^2\bigr]+\mathbb E\bigl[(M-c)^2\bigr].
$$

**Step 4: the inequality and the equality condition.** Since $(M-c)^2\ge 0$ pointwise, $\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]\ge 0$, and therefore
$$
\mathbb E\bigl[(X-c)^2\bigr]\ge\mathbb E\bigl[(X-M)^2\bigr].
$$
Equality holds exactly when $\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]=0$. Grouping by cells,
$$
\mathbb E\bigl[(M-c)^2\bigr]=\sum_{j=1}^m p_j(\mu_j-c)^2.
$$
This is a sum of nonnegative terms, so it is zero exactly when $p_j(\mu_j-c)^2=0$ for every $j$. For a cell with $p_j>0$ this means $\mu_j=c$. For a cell with $p_j=0$ the term is zero whatever $\mu_j$ is, so the convention $\mu_j=0$ puts no condition on $c$. Hence equality holds exactly when $\mu_j=c$ for every $j$ with $p_j>0$, that is, when $M=c$ on every cell of positive probability. The union of the remaining cells has probability zero, so this says precisely that $M=c$ with probability one. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Proof.** All expectations are finite sums over outcomes, for example $\mathbb E[Z]=\sum_{\omega}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})Z(\omega)$. Since each $\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\ge 0$ and $p_j=\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})$, a cell with $p_j=0$ has $\mathbb P(\{\omega\})=0$ for every $\omega\in G_j$. So every outcome in such a cell has weight zero in every expectation below, whatever value $M$ takes there.

**Step 1: the residual has conditional mean zero on each cell of positive probability.** Fix $j$ with $p_j>0$. On $G_j$ we have $M=\mu_j$, and the definition of $\mu_j$ gives

$$
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega)=p_j\mu_j .
$$

Therefore

$$
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-M(\omega)\bigr)
= p_j\mu_j-\mu_j p_j = 0 .
\tag{1}
$$

Dividing by $p_j$, this says $\mathbb E[X-M\mid G_j]=0$. This is the only property of the residual we use. We do not claim that $X-M$ is independent of $M$.

**Step 2: the cross term vanishes.** Group the sum defining $\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]$ by cells:

$$
\mathbb E\bigl[(X-M)(M-c)\bigr]
=\sum_{j=1}^m\ \sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-M(\omega)\bigr)\bigl(M(\omega)-c\bigr).
$$

Every term in a cell with $p_j=0$ has weight $\mathbb P(\{\omega\})=0$, so those cells contribute nothing, and the sum runs only over $j$ with $p_j>0$. On such a cell $M=\mu_j$ is constant, so the factor $\mu_j-c$ comes out of the inner sum, and (1) applies:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\bigl[(X-M)(M-c)\bigr]
&=\sum_{j:\,p_j>0}(\mu_j-c)\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-M(\omega)\bigr)\\
&=\sum_{j:\,p_j>0}(\mu_j-c)\cdot 0\\
&=0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: the identity.** Pointwise on the space,

$$
X-c=(X-M)+(M-c),
$$

and squaring gives

$$
(X-c)^2=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2 .
$$

Taking expectations is linear for finite sums, so by Step 2

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\bigl[(X-c)^2\bigr]
&=\mathbb E\bigl[(X-M)^2\bigr]+2\,\mathbb E\bigl[(X-M)(M-c)\bigr]+\mathbb E\bigl[(M-c)^2\bigr]\\
&=\mathbb E\bigl[(X-M)^2\bigr]+\mathbb E\bigl[(M-c)^2\bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4: the inequality and its equality case.** Since $(M-c)^2\ge 0$ pointwise, $\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]\ge 0$, and the identity gives

$$
\mathbb E\bigl[(X-c)^2\bigr]\ge \mathbb E\bigl[(X-M)^2\bigr].
$$

Equality holds exactly when $\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]=0$. Grouping by cells and again discarding the cells with $p_j=0$,

$$
\mathbb E\bigl[(M-c)^2\bigr]
=\sum_{j:\,p_j>0}\ \sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})(\mu_j-c)^2
=\sum_{j:\,p_j>0}p_j(\mu_j-c)^2 .
$$

This is a sum of nonnegative terms with $p_j>0$, so it is zero exactly when $\mu_j=c$ for every $j$ with $p_j>0$. The set $\{M\ne c\}$ is the union of the cells with $\mu_j\ne c$, so its probability is $\sum_{j:\,\mu_j\ne c}p_j$. That sum is zero exactly when every cell with $\mu_j\ne c$ has $p_j=0$, which is the condition just derived. Hence equality holds exactly when $\mathbb P(M=c)=1$. The arbitrary value $\mu_j=0$ assigned to zero-probability cells has no effect on this conclusion. $\qquad\blacksquare$

Of the 600 households invited to take part in the library-use survey, 360 returned the initial questionnaire. Among these respondents, 252 reported using a library in the previous month: 70 percent. This percentage described the initial respondents, as the preliminary note stated. It did not establish the percentage among all invited households, although it was sometimes interpreted that way.

The telephone follow-up added information from 90 of the 240 initial nonrespondents. Of those interviewed, 42, or approximately 46.7 percent, reported library use. These households were not selected through a simple random sample. Interviewers continued contact attempts until the budgeted 90 interviews were complete, so inclusion depended on both reaching a household and obtaining its agreement.

Combining the two stages gives 294 reports of library use among 450 responding households, or approximately 65.3 percent. The decline from 70 to 65.3 percent shows how the descriptive result changed when more households answered. It also shows that the initial respondents and the households reached in the follow-up differed in their reports.

The follow-up does not establish library-use prevalence among all 600 invitees. The remaining 150 households supplied no response, and we do not know whether their library use resembles that of either responding group. Although both stages used the same question and reference month, mode was not experimentally assigned. The difference between stages therefore cannot be separated into an effect of telephone interviewing and a difference in the households reached.

The follow-up broadened the observed group, but it did not demonstrate that nonresponse had been statistically corrected. Such a claim would require assumptions that were not evaluated here; no weights or imputed responses were used. The report should retain both stages and present 65.3 percent as the combined respondent percentage, alongside the uncertainty about the households still unobserved.

# What the Follow-Up Changes and What Remains Unknown

An early return rate can look like an answer to a question it has not answered. In our survey of library use, 600 households were invited and 360 returned the initial questionnaire. Of those 360, 252 reported using a library in the previous month, which is 70 percent of initial respondents. This figure appeared in the preliminary note, which described it as a finding about respondents. In later discussion it was sometimes treated as a description of all invited households, and that reading is not supported.

**What the follow-up added.** We approached the 240 initial nonrespondents by telephone. The follow-up budget covered 90 completed interviews, and interviewers worked through contact attempts until 90 were done. The 90 households are therefore not a simple random sample of the 240. Which households entered the group depended on whether interviewers could reach them and whether they agreed to take part. Forty-two of the 90 reported library use in the previous month, about 46.7 percent. The question and reference month were the same as in the questionnaire, but mode was not randomly assigned.

Combining the two stages gives 294 reports of library use among 450 responding households, about 65.3 percent. The shift from 70 to 65.3 percent is a change in the observed respondent pool. It shows that the initial respondents and the reached follow-up respondents differed in what they reported, and this is the concrete information the follow-up contributed.

**What the follow-up does not settle.** The combined figure does not tell us the prevalence among all 600 invitees, because 150 households still gave no response. It also cannot separate two explanations for the gap between 70 and 46.7 percent. One is a telephone-mode effect on how people answered. The other is a real difference between the people who answered by questionnaire and the people reached by phone. Without random assignment of mode, the two are entangled.

**Not an adjustment for nonresponse.** We considered describing the follow-up as an adjustment for nonresponse. In a descriptive sense it does broaden the observed group by including people absent from the first calculation. In the statistical sense, though, saying the remaining nonresponse has been corrected would require assumptions that we have not evaluated. No weights or imputed responses were used, and the combined figure should not be read as a corrected estimate.

**Recommendation for reporting.** The report should keep both stages visible rather than replacing the first percentage with a supposedly final population estimate:

| Stage | Households | Reported library use | Percent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial questionnaire | 360 | 252 | 70.0 |
| Telephone follow-up | 90 | 42 | about 46.7 |
| Combined respondents | 450 | 294 | about 65.3 |
| No response | 150 | unknown | unknown |

We do not know whether the 150 remaining households resemble either responding group. The combined figure should be accompanied by a plain statement of that uncertainty. The statement should not obscure what the follow-up showed: the descriptive result moved noticeably once a different group answered.

Let \(N\ge 2\), and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_N\) be fixed real responses. Define
\[
\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,
\qquad
\sigma^2=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Choose an unordered pair \(P\) uniformly from the \(\binom N2\) possible pairs, then choose an index \(J\) uniformly from the two indices in \(P\). Set
\[
Y=y_J,
\qquad
Z=\frac12\sum_{i\in P}y_i.
\]
All expectations and variances below refer to repeated sampling from this fixed population. We show that
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]

Each index belongs to \(N-1\) pairs. Thus, for every \(i\),
\[
\Pr(J=i)=\frac{N-1}{\binom N2}\cdot\frac12=\frac1N.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2.
\]

Conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the variable \(Y\) takes the values \(y_i\) and \(y_j\) with equal probabilities, while \(Z=(y_i+y_j)/2\) is fixed. Hence
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z.
\]
Taking expectations gives
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid P]\right]
=\mathbb E[Y]=\mu.
\]
The same conditional identity implies
\[
\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]=0.
\]
Because \(Z-\mu\) is determined by \(P\), it can be taken outside the conditional expectation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P]\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\right]
=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the two terms in \(Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu)\) have zero expected cross-product. Expanding the square and using \(\mathbb E[Z]=\mu\) yields
\[
\sigma^2
=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]
=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\]
This is an orthogonality argument; it does not require independence of \(Y\) and \(Z\).

To evaluate the remaining expectation, observe that, conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the two possible values of \(Y-Z\) are \((y_i-y_j)/2\) and its negative. Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
\]
Averaging over the uniformly selected pairs gives
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{1}{4\binom N2}\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2.
\]
The finite-population identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=N\sum_i y_i^2-\left(\sum_i y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2
=N^2\sigma^2
\end{aligned}
\]
then implies
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]

# Appendix: Mean and variance of the pair-mean estimator

**Setup.** Let N ≥ 2 and let y₁, …, y_N be fixed real numbers. Define

μ = N⁻¹ Σᵢ yᵢ and σ² = N⁻¹ Σᵢ (yᵢ − μ)².

Draw an unordered pair P uniformly from the C(N,2) pairs of indices. Then draw J uniformly from the two indices in P. Set

Y = y_J and Z = ½ Σ_{i∈P} yᵢ.

**Claim.** E[Z] = μ and Var(Z) = (N−2)σ² / (2(N−1)).

All randomness comes from the sampling design (P and J). The responses yᵢ are fixed constants, so the expectations and variances describe repeated sampling from this population.

The proof compares Y, a single draw, with Z, the mean of the pair containing it. Y and Z are dependent, since Z is determined by P and Y is drawn from within P. The argument never needs them to be independent, only a conditional-mean identity.

## Step 1: Y is a uniform draw from the population

Each index i lies in exactly N−1 of the C(N,2) pairs, so P(i ∈ P) = (N−1)/C(N,2) = 2/N. Given i ∈ P, J = i with probability 1/2. Hence

P(J = i) = (2/N)(1/2) = 1/N for every i.

So Y is a simple random draw from {y₁, …, y_N}, and

E[Y] = μ, Var(Y) = E[(Y−μ)²] = σ².

## Step 2: Conditional on the pair

Fix P = {i, j}. Given P, Y equals yᵢ or yⱼ with probability ½ each. Therefore

E[Y | P] = (yᵢ + yⱼ)/2 = Z,

and, since Y − Z = ±(yᵢ − yⱼ)/2,

E[(Y−Z)² | P = {i,j}] = (yᵢ − yⱼ)² / 4.

## Step 3: The mean of Z

By the first identity in Step 2 and the tower property,

E[Z] = E[E[Y | P]] = E[Y] = μ.

## Step 4: Decomposing σ²

Write Y − μ = (Y − Z) + (Z − μ) and square:

E[(Y−μ)²] = E[(Y−Z)²] + 2E[(Y−Z)(Z−μ)] + E[(Z−μ)²].

The cross term vanishes. Z − μ is a function of P, so it can be taken outside the conditional expectation:

E[(Y−Z)(Z−μ)] = E[(Z−μ) · E[Y−Z | P]] = E[(Z−μ) · 0] = 0.

This uses only E[Y − Z | P] = 0 from Step 2, not independence of Y and Z. Since E[Z] = μ, the last term is Var(Z). With Step 1, this gives

σ² = E[(Y−Z)²] + Var(Z). (1)

## Step 5: Computing E[(Y−Z)²]

Averaging the second identity in Step 2 over the C(N,2) equally likely pairs gives

E[(Y−Z)²] = (1 / (4·C(N,2))) Σ_{i<j} (yᵢ − yⱼ)².

For the sum, note that Σ_{i<j} = ½ Σᵢ Σⱼ, so

Σ_{i<j} (yᵢ − yⱼ)² = ½ Σᵢ Σⱼ (yᵢ² − 2yᵢyⱼ + yⱼ²)
 = N Σᵢ yᵢ² − (Σᵢ yᵢ)²
 = N [Σᵢ yᵢ² − Nμ²]
 = N Σᵢ (yᵢ − μ)²
 = N² σ².

Since 4·C(N,2) = 2N(N−1),

E[(Y−Z)²] = N²σ² / (2N(N−1)) = Nσ² / (2(N−1)). (2)

## Step 6: Conclusion

Substituting (2) into (1):

Var(Z) = σ² − Nσ² / (2(N−1)) = σ² · (2(N−1) − N) / (2(N−1)) = (N−2)σ² / (2(N−1)). ∎

Let x̂ be any minimizer of ‖Az − y‖₂ over z ∈ ℝ^d. A minimizer exists because the range of A is a subspace of ℝ^r, which is closed, so it contains a point nearest to y. We claim

$$
\|P(\hat x - x)\|_2 \le \frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}.
$$

This bounds only the component of the error in K^⊥. The matrix A does not see the component in K, and nothing here bounds it.

**Step 1: a bound on Ah.** Put h = x̂ − x. Since x̂ minimizes the quadratic ‖Az − y‖₂², its gradient vanishes there, which gives the normal equations Aᵀ(Ax̂ − y) = 0. Because y = Ax + e,

$$
A\hat x - y = A(\hat x - x) - e = Ah - e,
$$

so

$$
A^\top (Ah - e) = 0 .
$$

Multiplying on the left by hᵀ and using Cauchy–Schwarz,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|Ah\|_2^2 &= \langle Ah, e\rangle \\
&\le \|Ah\|_2 \,\|e\|_2 \\
&\le \|Ah\|_2\, \varepsilon .
\end{aligned}
$$

If Ah ≠ 0, dividing by ‖Ah‖₂ gives ‖Ah‖₂ ≤ ε. If Ah = 0, the same inequality holds trivially. In both cases

$$
\|Ah\|_2 \le \varepsilon. \tag{1}
$$

**Step 2: passing to the component in K^⊥.** The lower bound on A applies only to vectors in K^⊥, and h need not lie there. So we split h as

$$
h = Ph + (I-P)h .
$$

Here (I − P)h is the orthogonal projection of h onto K, hence A(I − P)h = 0. Therefore

$$
Ah = A Ph + A(I-P)h = A Ph. \tag{2}
$$

Since Ph ∈ K^⊥, the assumed lower bound applies to it. Combining it with (2) and (1),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma \|Ph\|_2 &\le \|A Ph\|_2 \\
&= \|Ah\|_2 \\
&\le \varepsilon .
\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by γ > 0 gives

$$
\|P(\hat x - x)\|_2 = \|Ph\|_2 \le \frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma},
$$

which is the claim. ∎

**Special cases.**

- If ε = 0, the bound gives P(x̂ − x) = 0, so the component of x̂ in K^⊥ equals that of x. The minimizer need not be unique, because x̂ + k is also a minimizer for every k ∈ K.
- If K^⊥ = {0}, then P = 0 and the claim is trivial. The hypothesis on γ holds vacuously.

**Setup.** Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times d}$, $x\in\mathbb R^d$, and $y=Ax+e$ with $\|e\|_2\le\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon\ge 0$. Let $K=\{v\in\mathbb R^d: Av=0\}$ and let $P$ be the orthogonal projection onto $K^\perp$. Assume $\gamma>0$ and

$$
\|Av\|_2\ \ge\ \gamma\|v\|_2\qquad\text{for every } v\in K^\perp .
$$

Components in $K$ are not determined by the observations. Let $\hat x$ be any minimizer of $\|Az-y\|_2$ over $z\in\mathbb R^d$. A minimizer exists because $A\mathbb R^d$ is a subspace of $\mathbb R^r$, so $y$ has a nearest point $Az$ in it. We claim

$$
\|P(\hat x-x)\|_2\ \le\ \frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}.
$$

This bounds only the observable component of the error. Nothing is claimed about the component in $K$.

**Step 1: the residual of the error is orthogonal to the range of $A$.** The function $z\mapsto\|Az-y\|_2^2$ is differentiable and is minimized at $\hat x$, so its gradient vanishes there:

$$
A^\top(A\hat x-y)=0 .
$$

Put $h=\hat x-x$. Since $y=Ax+e$, we have $A\hat x-y=Ah-e$, and therefore

$$
A^\top(Ah-e)=0 .
$$

**Step 2: $\|Ah\|_2\le\varepsilon$.** Multiplying on the left by $h^\top$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 &= h^\top A^\top(Ah-e)\\
  &= \langle Ah,\,Ah-e\rangle ,
\end{aligned}
$$

so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|Ah\|_2^2 &= \langle Ah,e\rangle\\
&\le \|Ah\|_2\,\|e\|_2 &&\text{(Cauchy–Schwarz)}\\
&\le \|Ah\|_2\,\varepsilon .
\end{aligned}
$$

If $Ah\neq 0$, dividing by $\|Ah\|_2$ gives $\|Ah\|_2\le\varepsilon$. If $Ah=0$, then $\|Ah\|_2=0\le\varepsilon$ holds trivially.

**Step 3: the observation of $h$ depends only on $Ph$.** The lower bound holds only on $K^\perp$, and $h$ need not lie in $K^\perp$. Decompose

$$
h = Ph + (I-P)h ,
$$

where $(I-P)$ is the orthogonal projection onto $K$, so $(I-P)h\in K$ and $A(I-P)h=0$. Then

$$
Ah = A\,Ph + A(I-P)h = A\,Ph .
$$

**Step 4: apply the lower bound to $Ph$.** Since $Ph\in K^\perp$, the assumption applies to $v=Ph$. Combining it with Steps 3 and 2,

$$
\gamma\|Ph\|_2\ \le\ \|A\,Ph\|_2\ =\ \|Ah\|_2\ \le\ \varepsilon .
$$

Dividing by $\gamma>0$,

$$
\|P(\hat x-x)\|_2=\|Ph\|_2\ \le\ \frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}. \qquad\blacksquare
$$

**Remarks on the cases.**

- If $\varepsilon=0$, Step 2 gives $Ah=0$, so $h\in K$ and $Ph=0$. The observable component of $x$ is recovered exactly. This does not make $\hat x$ unique, since $\hat x$ may differ from $x$ by any element of $K$.
- If $K^\perp=\{0\}$, then $P=0$, the hypothesis on $K^\perp$ is vacuous, and the claim holds trivially.
- The proof never uses invertibility of $A$. The component $(I-P)\hat x-(I-P)x$ in $K$ is not bounded, because $A$ gives no information about it.

At the start of each shift, place the probe in the reference fixture and record its reading. The acceptance band is 48 to 52 units, including both endpoints. This check compares the probe with a stable reference block. It does not measure the temperature of material currently on the line, and a reading inside the band does not by itself authorize a production restart.

During the six-week trial, if the first reference-block reading is outside the acceptance band, repeat the reading once after the probe has rested in the fixture for ten minutes. Record both readings in the shift log. If the repeat is also outside the band, call the shift lead; if the repeat is within the band, no call is required by this rule. The ten-minute rest applies only before the repeat; the start-of-shift check and acceptance band are unchanged. The lead will decide whether a further check is needed. Do not change the probe's offset in response to this check. The trial concerns the escalation process, not permission for operators to recalibrate the instrument.

For the weekly trend chart, use the first reading from each shift, including first readings outside the acceptance band. Keep any repeat readings in the log, but do not substitute them into the chart. This keeps the plotted sequence tied to the same point in the checking process, even when the escalation procedure calls for more than one observation.

The maintenance team will review the log and the chart at the end of the trial. A charted outlier is a reason to examine the record, not a diagnosis of a failed probe. Please include notes about a loose fixture or an interrupted check where relevant. Those notes help explain what happened, but they do not replace the numerical readings.
